question.name: Questions: a rising voice or a question word
question.about: A yes/no question keeps the order of a statement, with the voice rising on the word asked about (Ты говори́шь по-англи́йски?), a question word like как, где or что often comes first, and Russian adds no do.

source.note: First drafted by Lexicommons, open to correction. Short name and one-line rule added in revision 2.

question.short: A yes/no question keeps a statement's order, the voice rising: Маши́на здесь? (car here?). A question word most often comes first: Где маши́на?

no-be.name: No am, is or are in the present
no-be.about: Russian leaves out am, is and are in the present: Я студе́нт (I'm a student); Где мои́ ключи́? (Where are my keys?).

source.note: First drafted by Lexicommons, open to correction. Short name and one-line rule added in revision 2.

no-be.short: Russian leaves out am, is and are in the present: Я до́ма (I at home: I'm at home), Где ключ? (where key?).

have.name: Having: у меня́ есть
have.about: To say you have something, Russian says it is at you: У меня́ есть брат (I have a brother); when what matters is what it's like, not whether it's there, есть is often left out: У меня́ больша́я ко́мната.

source.note: First drafted by Lexicommons, open to correction. Short name and one-line rule added in revision 2.

have.short: To have is to be at you: У меня́ есть рабо́та (at me is work: I have work); with none, нет and the genitive: У меня́ нет рабо́ты.

present.name: Present tense endings
present.about: The verb changes for each person: я живу́, ты живёшь, он живёт, мы живём, они́ живу́т.

source.note: First drafted by Lexicommons, open to correction. Short name and one-line rule added in revision 2.

present.short: The verb's ending says who: я пью, ты пьёшь, он пьёт (I drink, you drink, he drinks).

infinitive.name: When the next verb is an infinitive
infinitive.about: After words like мо́жешь, хочу́, люблю́, дай and пора́, the next verb stays in its dictionary form: мо́жешь закры́ть, хочу́ съесть, дай знать, пора́ идти́.

source.note: First drafted by Lexicommons, open to correction. Short name and one-line rule added in revision 2.

infinitive.short: After хочу́, могу́ and the like, the next verb stays in its dictionary form: Я хочу́ пить (I want drink), Я могу́ помо́чь.

plural.name: Plurals
plural.about: In their basic (nominative) form, plural nouns mostly end in -ы or -и, or -а or -я (ключи́, дела́); adjectives and possessives such as мой take plural forms too (но́вые, мои́), and some meanings are normally plural (выходны́е, the weekend).

source.note: First drafted by Lexicommons, open to correction. Short name and one-line rule added in revision 2.

plural.short: Most plurals end in -ы or -и, some in -а or -я: ключи́, маши́ны, дела́.

gender.name: Masculine, feminine, neuter
gender.about: Most nouns ending in a consonant are masculine, most in -а or -я feminine and most in -о or -е neuter (though words for men stay masculine: па́па), and adjectives, possessives such as мой and a singular past-tense verb agree with them.

source.note: First drafted by Lexicommons, open to correction. Short name and one-line rule added in revision 2.

gender.short: Most nouns are он words, она́ words or оно́ words, and words with them match: мой телефо́н, моя́ су́мка, моё молоко́.

adjective.name: Adjectives match
adjective.about: An adjective matches its noun's gender, number and case: но́вый дом, но́вая ку́ртка, но́вые боти́нки, в ма́ленькой кварти́ре.

source.note: First drafted by Lexicommons, open to correction. Short name and one-line rule added in revision 2.

adjective.short: An adjective matches its noun's gender, number and case: но́вый дом, но́вая маши́на, в но́вой маши́не.

accusative.name: The accusative: objects, where you go, when
accusative.about: A direct object often takes the accusative (Мы е́ли пи́ццу); so does where you're going after в or на (в магази́н, на рабо́ту), and many expressions of time (в суббо́ту).

source.note: First drafted by Lexicommons, open to correction. Short name and one-line rule added in revision 2.

accusative.short: What you drink, read or see takes the accusative; for -а words it ends in -у: Я пью во́ду, Я чита́ю кни́гу.

genitive.name: Of, without: the genitive
genitive.about: The genitive can mean of (маши́на па́пы, ча́шка ча́я), follows без, из and у, and comes after many amounts and numbers: без са́хара, де́сять мину́т.

source.note: First drafted by Lexicommons, open to correction. Short name and one-line rule added in revision 2.

genitive.short: The genitive says of, and follows для, без, из and у: маши́на ма́мы (car of Mom), для ма́мы, у меня́.

genitive-negation.name: нет + genitive
genitive-negation.about: To say there isn't something, use нет and the genitive: нет молока́, У меня́ нет вре́мени; and не бу́дет for the future.

source.note: First drafted by Lexicommons, open to correction. Short name and one-line rule added in revision 2.

genitive-negation.short: With нет, what isn't there takes the genitive: У меня́ нет рабо́ты (at me no work), нет молока́.

prepositional.name: Where and how: в or на + prepositional
prepositional.about: With в or на, where something is takes the prepositional, usually ending in -е: в Москве́, на столе́, в холоди́льнике; and how you travel: на авто́бусе.

source.note: First drafted by Lexicommons, open to correction. Short name and one-line rule added in revision 2.

prepositional.short: After в and на, where something is mostly ends in -е: на столе́, в су́мке, в маши́не.

dative.name: To someone: the dative
dative.about: The dative is to or for someone: Я позвоню́ тебе́; and the one who feels or likes: Мне хо́лодно (I'm cold), Мне нра́вится (I like it).

source.note: First drafted by Lexicommons, open to correction. Short name and one-line rule added in revision 2.

dative.short: The dative says to or for someone, and who feels something: Я дам тебе́ (I'll give you), Мне хо́лодно (to me cold: I'm cold).

instrumental.name: With, as, and за
instrumental.about: The instrumental follows с (with: с ма́мой), says what you work as (Я рабо́таю врачо́м), and follows за for going to get something (за хле́бом).

source.note: First drafted by Lexicommons, open to correction. Short name and one-line rule added in revision 2.

instrumental.short: After с (with), a word takes the instrumental: ко́фе с молоко́м (coffee with milk), со мной (with me).

direction.name: Where you are, where you go
direction.about: Going and being somewhere differ: куда́ and где, домо́й and до́ма, сюда́ and здесь; в магази́н (to the store) but в магази́не (in the store).

source.note: First drafted by Lexicommons, open to correction. Short name and one-line rule added in revision 2.

direction.short: Being somewhere and going there are different words: до́ма (at home), домо́й (home, going there); здесь and сюда́.

ne.name: не before what it denies
ne.about: не (not) goes right before the word it denies, and stays even with никогда́ (never): Я не зна́ю; Я никогда́ не был.

source.note: First drafted by Lexicommons, open to correction. Short name and one-line rule added in revision 2.

ne.short: не goes right before what it denies: Я не пью ко́фе (I not drink coffee). There's no do.

past.name: Past tense by gender
past.about: The past says the gender in the singular, not the person (он был, она́ была́, они́ бы́ли; a woman says я купи́ла, a man я купи́л), and some pasts describe how things are now: ты уста́л (you're tired).

source.note: First drafted by Lexicommons, open to correction. Short name and one-line rule added in revision 2.

past.short: The past says the gender, not the person: он был, она́ была́, они́ бы́ли; a woman says я была́.

future.name: Talking about the future
future.about: Use бу́ду and an imperfective infinitive for an action seen as ongoing, repeated or not about finishing it (never бу́ду купи́ть); the present for a plan (За́втра я е́ду на рабо́ту); бу́дет for what there will be (За́втра бу́дет дождь); a present-looking perfective for one whole action (Я позвоню́); and the future after е́сли too (Е́сли не бу́дет дождя́, мы пойдём на пляж).

source.note: First drafted by Lexicommons, open to correction. Short name and one-line rule added in revision 2.

future.short: бу́ду with an infinitive for what will be going on (Я бу́ду чита́ть); a perfective verb's present form for what will get done (Я прочита́ю).

aspect.name: Two verbs for one action
aspect.about: Many verbs come in pairs: one for an action going on or repeated (покупа́ть, звони́ть), one for the action as one finished whole (купи́ть, позвони́ть).

source.note: First drafted by Lexicommons, open to correction. Short name and one-line rule added in revision 2.

aspect.short: Most verbs come in pairs: one for going on or again (чита́ть), one for done once (прочита́ть).

motion.name: Going: идти́ or е́хать
motion.about: For one trip, going now or planned, идти́ is going on foot (and coming or leaving: Иди́ сюда́; Мне пора́ идти́) and е́хать going by car, bus or train; ходи́ть and е́здить are for regular trips, or there and back; пойти́ and пое́хать set off on one trip.

source.note: First drafted by Lexicommons, open to correction. Short name and one-line rule added in revision 2.

motion.short: идти́ is going on foot, е́хать going in something; for one trip now or planned: Я иду́ домо́й, Я е́ду домо́й.

new-last.name: What's new goes last
new-last.about: Russian order is free-ish, and the new information often comes late, so the subject can follow the verb: На столе́ лежи́т кни́га (on the table lies a book).

source.note: First drafted by Lexicommons, open to correction. Short name and one-line rule added in revision 2.

new-last.short: What's new often comes last, so the subject can follow the verb: На столе́ лежи́т ключ (on the table lies a key).

address.name: Informal ты, polite вы
address.about: ты and its verb forms speak to one person you know well, and вы and its forms to several people or politely to one, such as a waiter, a stranger or an older adult (Принеси́те, пожа́луйста; Извини́те), so use вы with an adult you don't know until they offer ты.

source.note: First drafted by Lexicommons, open to correction. Short name and one-line rule added in revision 2.

address.short: ты is for one person you know well, вы for someone you don't or for more than one, with the plural verb: Вы идёте домо́й?

imperative.name: Telling someone to do something
imperative.about: The command form has its own ending and no subject: Закро́й дверь! Иди́ сюда́! Дай мне знать! (-те for more people or politely: Принеси́те.)

source.note: First drafted by Lexicommons, open to correction. Short name and one-line rule added in revision 2.

imperative.short: The command form has no subject: Иди́ домо́й! Дай мне ключ! For вы, -те: Иди́те домо́й!

possessive.name: My, your: мой, твой
possessive.about: мой (my) and твой (your) match their noun like an adjective: мой ключ, моя́ су́мка, моё молоко́, мои́ ключи́. его́ (his), её (her) and их (their) never change: его́ маши́на, её телефо́н.

source.note: First drafted by Lexicommons, open to correction. Added in revision 2 for lessons 1–20.

possessive.short: мой and твой match their noun: мой ключ, моя́ су́мка, моё молоко́; его́, её and их never change.

demonstrative.name: This: э́тот, э́то
demonstrative.about: э́тот (this) matches its noun: э́тот телефо́н, э́та су́мка, э́то молоко́. э́то on its own says this is or it's, with no is: Э́то мой ключ (this my key: this is my key).

source.note: First drafted by Lexicommons, open to correction. Added in revision 2 for lessons 1–20.

demonstrative.short: э́тот matches its noun (э́тот телефо́н, э́та су́мка); э́то alone says this is: Э́то мой ключ (this my key).

short-adjective.name: Ready, glad: short adjectives
short-adjective.about: A few adjectives have a short form for how someone is, and like the past it says the gender: Я гото́в (I'm ready, a man says), Я гото́ва (a woman says), Мы гото́вы (we're ready).

source.note: First drafted by Lexicommons, open to correction. Added in revision 2 for lessons 1–20.

short-adjective.short: A few adjectives have a short form for how someone is, and it says the gender: Я гото́в (a man), Я гото́ва (a woman), Мы гото́вы.

question-word.name: Who, what, where: question words
question-word.about: Кто asks who, что what, где where, куда́ where to, отку́да where from, когда́ when and почему́ why. The question word usually comes first; the subject or verb can follow: Куда́ ты идёшь? Куда́ идёт твой друг? With кто as the subject, use the singular third-person verb: Кто стучи́т?

source.note: Written with the Russian lessons 21–40, open to correction.

question-word.short: Usually put the question word first: Что ты и́щешь? Где asks where someone is, куда́ where they are going, отку́да where they are coming from. No do is added.

pronoun-object.name: The person you hear or see: object pronouns
pronoun-object.about: The person heard or seen takes the accusative object form: я → меня́, ты → тебя́, он → его́, она́ → её, мы → нас, вы → вас, они́ → их. The object often comes before the verb: Ты меня́ слы́шишь? Я тебя́ ви́жу. The form, rather than a fixed position, shows who is heard or seen.

source.note: Written with the Russian lessons 21–40, open to correction.

pronoun-object.short: For the person heard or seen, use меня́, тебя́, его́, её, нас, вас or их: Ты меня́ слы́шишь? Я её ви́жу. These forms often come before the verb.

ni-ne.name: Nothing and never: ни with не
ni-ne.about: Ничего́ and никогда́ normally go with не before a finite verb: Я ничего́ не хочу́; Я никогда́ не пью ко́фе. These words express one negative meaning together. Ничего́ means nothing or, with not in English, anything; никогда́ means never. Нет can itself supply the negative in a statement about absence.

source.note: Written with the Russian lessons 41–60, open to correction.

ni-ne.short: Keep не before the verb with ничего́ and никогда́: Я ничего́ не зна́ю; Я никогда́ не пью ко́фе.

chto-clause.name: What someone thinks or says: что
chto-clause.about: Что links a statement to a verb such as ду́мать, говори́ть or знать: Я ду́маю, что ма́ма уже́ до́ма. Each clause keeps its own subject and agreement: Я зна́ю, что ты рабо́таешь. Write a comma before что. Time and place can follow in the ordinary order for the meaning you want.

source.note: Written with the Russian lessons 41–60, open to correction.

chto-clause.short: Use что to introduce what someone says, thinks or knows: Я зна́ю, что ма́ма до́ма. Each clause has its own subject; no English-style do is added.

because.name: Giving a reason: потому́ что
because.about: Потому́ что introduces the reason: Я опа́здываю, потому́ что не могу́ найти́ ключ. Почему́ asks why; потому́ что gives the reason. Normally put a comma before the whole phrase. Both parts keep their usual statements and verb forms.

source.note: Written with the Russian lessons 41–60, open to correction.

because.short: Answer почему́ with потому́ что and a reason: Ма́ма опа́здывает, потому́ что не мо́жет найти́ телефо́н.

verb-case.name: Learn the case with the verb
verb-case.about: A verb helps choose the form of the person it concerns: Я жду тебя́, but Я помога́ю тебе́. Ждать takes the accusative for the person waited for; помога́ть and помо́чь take the dative for the person helped. English for after wait does not mean Russian needs a preposition here. Learn any preposition a different verb needs together with that verb.

source.note: Written with the Russian lessons 41–60, open to correction.

verb-case.short: For a person, learn ждать + тебя́ and помога́ть or помо́чь + тебе́: Я жду тебя́; Я помога́ю тебе́.

genitive-plural.name: Years and money: the genitive plural
genitive-plural.about: Use the genitive plural after пять or ско́лько when counting years: пять лет, ско́лько лет. The person whose age you give is in the dative: Ему́ пять лет. Нет takes the genitive too: У меня́ нет де́нег. Learn each noun’s form; there is no single ending for every noun.

source.note: Written with the Russian lessons 61–80, open to correction.

genitive-plural.short: After пять or ско́лько, years is лет: Ему́ пять лет. The genitive plural also follows нет for absent plural things: нет де́нег.

numbers.name: One, two, five: counting things
numbers.about: In a basic count, оди́н matches the noun: оди́н стол, одна́ кни́га. Два or две and три take the genitive singular: два стола́, две кни́ги. Пять takes the genitive plural: пять столо́в, пять книг. Use две with feminine nouns. A noun already understood can be left out: У меня́ две.

source.note: Written with the Russian lessons 61–80, open to correction.

numbers.short: Compare оди́н стол, два стола́, пять столо́в; одна́ кни́га, две кни́ги, пять книг. Два becomes две with a feminine noun. Leave out an understood noun: У меня́ две.

chtoby.name: In order to: что́бы
chtoby.about: Что́бы with an infinitive gives a purpose when the same person does both actions: Я иду́ в парк, что́бы гуля́ть. It says what the action is intended to achieve. Write a comma before что́бы. These examples keep the same doer; clauses with a different doer come later.

source.note: Written with the Russian lessons 61–80, open to correction.

chtoby.short: Use что́бы + infinitive for the purpose of the same person’s action: Мы идём домо́й, что́бы отдохну́ть. Put a comma before что́бы.

pronoun-cases.name: Pronouns in all six cases
pronoun-cases.about: A pronoun changes with its job: я as subject; у меня́ (genitive); ви́дит меня́ (accusative); помога́ет мне (dative); со мной (instrumental); обо мне (prepositional). Compare ты, тебя́, тебе́, тобо́й. The verb or preposition chooses the case. Обо is unstressed; in обо мне the stress is on мне.

source.note: Written with the Russian lessons 81–100, open to correction.

pronoun-cases.short: Follow the verb or preposition: ждёт меня́, помога́ет мне, со мной, обо мне. For ты, use тебя́, тебе́ or тобо́й as the job requires.

reflexive.name: Verbs with -ся and -сь
reflexive.about: Keep -ся or -сь attached when changing a verb: боя́ться → я бою́сь, ты бои́шься, он бои́тся. These endings belong to the word; they do not always mean yourself. Learn the whole verb and its meaning. In the forms here, use -сь after a vowel and -ся after a consonant letter or ь.

source.note: Written with the Russian lessons 81–100, open to correction.

reflexive.short: Keep the ending: я бою́сь, ты бои́шься. The person changes before -ся or -сь. The ending does not always mean yourself; learn the whole verb.

li.name: Whether: a question with ли
li.about: An embedded yes/no question uses ли after the word or group being questioned: Я не зна́ю, до́ма ли сестра́. Ли is not placed before the whole clause like English whether. Keep a question word when asking where or when: Ты зна́ешь, где мой телефо́н? Put a comma before the embedded question.

source.note: Written with the Russian lessons 81–100, open to correction.

li.short: Put ли after what is questioned: Я не зна́ю, до́ма ли сестра́. With a question word, keep that word: Ты зна́ешь, где мой телефо́н?

conditional.name: Would and could: бы
conditional.about: Use бы with a verb in its past form for an imagined possibility, a wish or a softened request: Мы могли́ бы позвони́ть за́втра; Я хоте́л бы помо́чь. The form still agrees with the person: мог бы, могла́ бы, могли́ бы. It need not refer to past time. Бы is a separate word and can move within the clause.

source.note: Written with the Russian lessons 101–120, open to correction.

conditional.short: Past form + бы: Вы могли́ бы мне помо́чь? Я хоте́л бы помо́чь тебе́. A woman says хоте́ла бы; with мы or вы, use хоте́ли бы or могли́ бы.

impersonal.name: A need or experience without a subject
impersonal.about: Russian can describe a need, experience or possibility without a nominative subject: Мне ну́жно учи́ться; Мне удо́бно чита́ть до́ма; Мо́жно учи́ться вме́сте. The person experiencing it is dative, and the describing word stays unchanged. Contrast Мне нужна́ кни́га: there кни́га is the subject and нужна́ agrees with it.

source.note: Written with the Russian lessons 101–120, open to correction.

impersonal.short: Use a dative person with an unchanged state word and, when needed, an infinitive: Мне удо́бно учи́ться до́ма. Мо́жно + infinitive expresses permission or possibility.
